 Moving to Israel? 10 tax moves every oleh should make before December 31
 As 2026 draws to a close, new immigrants face key deadlines to claim tax exemptions, protect foreign income, maximize credits and avoid costly mistakes; from salaries and stock options to property purchases and family gifts, her are 10 steps that could save you big 
 Attorney Amit Gottlieb | Add a comment Print Find an error? Report us Related Topics Immigration New immigrants Taxes Olim Aliyah Tax Authority For most olim, aliyah is a personal decision. For the Israel Tax Authority, it also marks the start of a new tax status, and that status comes with generous benefits: a ten-year exemption on foreign income and, for recent arrivals, a new exemption on income earned in Israel. None of this happens on its own. A great deal depends on decisions made before the move and in the first months after it, and with the 2026 tax year ending in a few weeks, several of those decisions now have a deadline. ( Photo: Shutterstock ) These are the points I would review with any oleh, or anyone planning aliyah, before December 31. 1. Arrived this year? Claim your exemption before December 31 
 If you arrived on or after November 5, 2025, your Israeli salary or business income may be tax-exempt. Your employer, however, can only apply the exemption once the Tax Authority approves a tax coordination request (Form 116ע). File now and the benefit can show up on your December payslip, rather than in a refund sometime in 2027. Self-employed individuals can ask to reduce their advance payments. Note that the exemption applies to work and business income only, not to interest, dividends, rent or capital gains. 2. Still abroad? The calendar matters 
 Following the dissolution of the Knesset, the window to qualify for the new exemption has been extended to February 10, 2027. Moving before December 31 still makes a difference, because only those who become residents in 2026 receive a share of the 2026 exemption. Arrive in January and that year is gone. After February 10, the window closes altogether. 3. Ten-year exemption ending in 2027? Act this year 
 If your ten-year exemption on foreign income ends next year, the coming weeks are the time to decide what to sell, withdraw or restructure while your Israeli tax is still zero. The ten years are counted from the day you became a resident, not from January 1, so if you arrived in June, the exemption ends in June. Ideally, this review should start a full year in advance. 4. Options and RSUs: December or January? 
 Equity received from a foreign employer is taxed according to when it was granted, when it vested and when it is sold, and according to how much of the work was done before and after aliyah. Part of the gain may receive favorable treatment, part will be taxed in Israel, and the country you left may claim its share as well. A sale on December 28 and a sale on January 3 can fall into different tax years, with very different results. 5. Check your December payslip 
 Olim receive additional tax credit points during their first four and a half years in Israel, and employers do not always apply them. December is the last opportunity to correct this within the year. If you started working mid-year or changed jobs, you may well have overpaid, and a refund can be claimed for previous years too. 6. Get your foreign records in order 
 Olim who arrived by the end of 2025 are exempt from reporting foreign income for ten years. Those who arrived in 2026 or later still pay no tax on it, but they are required to report it. Use the end of the year to list what was sold, distributed or withdrawn abroad, and to collect statements. Before winding up a company you owned before aliyah, even a dormant one, check whether it could give you a meaningful tax advantage. Attorney Amit Gottlieb Photo: Tomer Jacobson 7. Use your losses 
 Unused capital losses carry forward indefinitely and can be offset against future gains, including gains on real estate. Under Israeli case law, however, they cannot be inherited. They expire on death, while the heirs still pay tax on gains that accrued from the original purchase. Year-end is a sensible moment to review your portfolio and consider realizing gains against losses you have accumulated. Make sure those losses were reported in the year they arose, and avoid transactions that could be viewed as artificial. 8. Think twice before a family gift 
 Israel has no gift tax, but for olim a gift can sometimes cost the exemption. An asset an oleh bought before aliyah may be sold tax-free, while the same asset received as a gift may be fully taxable. Family transfers should be planned with this in mind. 9. Buying a home 
 Olim buying a home in Israel are entitled to a significant reduction in purchase tax, which on higher-priced properties can amount to substantial savings. The benefit is available once, from one year before aliyah until seven years after. 10. Plan the structure before you move 
 Most of the benefits available to olim depend on where things stand on the day you become a resident: what you own, how you hold it and how it came to you. A well-planned structure can secure years of exemption. Without one, the exemption may be lost, and often it cannot be recovered after the fact. This article is intended for general information only and does not constitute legal or tax advice. Every situation is different, and anyone considering these steps should seek professional advice tailored to their own circumstances. The author is a senior partner at YETAX, specializing in international taxation and HNW private client matters.
